direct_use_reviews.text: [F3] Absolutely integrable kernels permit Fubini and dominated convergence. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

proof_steps.claim: Let $\kappa_i$ be finitely many charts with smooth unitary frames, and let $\phi_i$ be a partition subordinate to compact subsets of those charts. Choose smooth cutoffs $\chi_i(y,z)$ supported where both points lie in chart $i$, equal to one near $y=z$ whenever $z\in\operatorname{supp}\phi_i$. Write volume as $w_i(z)\,d\kappa_i(z)$. Define $Z_t(y,z)$ in these frames by the finite sum of $\phi_i(z)\chi_i(y,z)w_i(z)^{-1}t^{-n/2}k_{i,z}((\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t)$, interpreting each summand as a bundle map. In each summand the principal coefficients are frozen at the source $z$. Step 1.1, local equivalence of chart distance and $d$, and cutoff support give $\|Z_t(y,z)\|\le C_LH_{t,L}(y,z)$, where $H_{t,L}=t^{-n/2}(1+d(y,z)/\sqrt t)^{-L}$. Moreover $Z_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$: put $\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z)=\sqrt t\,v$, use the uniform integrable Schwartz bound, and use $\sum_i\phi_i=1$ and $\int k_{i,y}=I$. For $R_t=(\partial_t+P_y)Z_t$, the frozen principal part cancels $\partial_t$. The remaining principal term contains $A(y)-A(z)=O(d(y,z))$ and two derivatives of the frozen kernel; lower terms contain at most one derivative. The bound $d(y,z)t^{-1}H_{t,L+1}\le t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ therefore gives $\|R_t(y,z)\|\le C_Lt^{-1/2}H_{t,L}(y,z)$. Derivatives of cutoffs are supported away from the diagonal and obey the same bound by choosing additional Schwartz decay.

Define Volterra convolution by $(A*B)_t(y,z)=\int_0^t\int_M A_{t-s}(y,u)B_s(u,z)\,du\,ds$. The residual bound and step 3.1 show $\|R*R\|\le C H_{t,L}$, since $\int_0^t((t-s)s)^{-1/2}\,ds=\pi$ (substitute $s=t\sin^2\theta$). Iterating this bounded time kernel gives $\|R^{*(2m)}_t\|\le C^{2m}t^{m-1}H_{t,L}/(m-1)!$ after enlarging $C$. Convolving once more with $R$ gives $\|R^{*(2m+1)}_t\|\le 2C^{2m+1}t^{m-1/2}H_{t,L}/(m-1)!$ for $m\ge1$, by bounding $s^{m-1}\le t^{m-1}$ in the time integral; $R$ itself has its original bound. Consequently $Q=\sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^mR^{*m}$ converges absolutely on every positive-time compact set, has $\|Q_t\|\le C t^{-1/2}H_{t,L}$ for $t\le1$, and satisfies $Q+R+R*Q=0$. Fubini and associativity hold because every displayed absolute convolution bound is finite. Hence $S=Z+Z*Q$ satisfies $\|S_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t H_{t,L}$ and $S_tf\to f$ in $L^2$ for smooth $f$.

Extend kernels causally by zero for negative time. The initial limit of $Z$ gives $(\partial_t+P_y)Z=\delta_0I+R$ in distributions. Applying this identity to the absolutely convergent convolutions of step 4.1 yields $(\partial_t+P_y)S=\delta_0I+R+Q+R*Q=\delta_0I$. These distribution identities can equivalently be verified first on $\varepsilon<s<t-\varepsilon$, tested against a compactly supported smooth function of time and space, and then passed to the endpoints using the integrable bounds from step 4.1. Thus no differentiation of a singular convolution is assumed pointwise. For smooth initial $f$, let $\psi$ be a smooth eigensection of $P$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. Formal symmetry and the distribution equation give $a'(t)+\lambda a(t)=0$ for $a(t)=\langle S_tf,\psi\rangle$, with $a(0)=\langle f,\psi\rangle$. Therefore $a(t)=e^{-t\lambda}\langle f,\psi\rangle$. The two-sided integral bounds in step 3.1 make $S_t$ bounded on $L^2$ (apply Cauchy–Schwarz with weight $\|S_t(y,z)\|$). Completeness of the given eigenbasis proves $S_t=e^{-tP}$ on $L^2$. The series and convolutions define continuous kernels for $t>0$: on time intervals away from the endpoints use uniform convergence, and bound the omitted endpoint intervals by the integrable convolution estimates. Equality as distributions with the smooth given $K_t$ therefore gives $S_t(y,z)=K_t(y,z)$ everywhere. In particular the bound for $S$ is the stated bound for $K$.

Fix $x$ and put $y=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,a)$, $z=\exp_x(\sqrt t\,b)$. In a chart, Taylor expansion gives $(\kappa_i(y)-\kappa_i(z))/\sqrt t\to d\kappa_i|_x(a-b)$, the frozen symbol tends to $p_i(x,\xi)$, and all frame maps, partition weights and density factors tend to their values at $x$. Linear change of cotangent variables in the absolutely convergent Fourier integral transforms each limiting chart expression into $\phi_i(x)k_x(a-b)$: the coordinate Jacobian cancels $w_i(x)$ because normal-coordinate volume density at $x$ is one. Summing gives $k_x(a-b)$. All convergences are uniform on bounded $a,b$ by step 1.1. By step 4.1, $t^{n/2}\|K_t-Z_t\|\le C\sqrt t$, so it has zero limit. This proves the rescaled limit and all assertions for $n>0$. If $M$ is empty the claims are vacuous; for $n=0$, compact $M$ is finite and differential operators act separately on its fibers, so ordinary matrix exponentiation gives exactly the asserted finite-dimensional limit.

Expanding $[B-g^2(\xi-s)]^2/(2g^2)$ gives $B^2/(2g^2)+g^2(\xi-s)^2/2+Bs-\xi B$. Step 1.1 shows all the required nonnegative densities are integrable. If $G(R)=\int_{|x|=R}(|Dq|^2+|Dp|^2)ds$, then [F9] and finite energy give $\int G(R)dR<\infty$. Hence there are increasing radii $R_j\to\infty$ with $R_jG(R_j)\to0$, since an eventual positive lower bound on $RG(R)$ would force logarithmic divergence. Uniform vacuum amplitudes and [F8] bound the boundary-current integral by $C\sqrt{R_jG(R_j)}\to0$. Integrating the two algebraic identities on those disks, using [F11], limiting flux $2\pi n$ and [F10] gives the stated whole-plane identity. For negative n, conjugation reverses flux and changes $D_1+iD_2$ to $D_1-iD_2$ without changing energy.

Step 1.1 makes the embedded three-dimensional energy exactly its mathematical critical energy. For arbitrary fixed full-model ends in the class [F7], specialize [F6] to linear u and constant $b=g^{-2}$; the nonzero c and closed valid disk meet its hypotheses. It constructs actual finite collars from both ends to the selected profile of step 3.1, with the same flux, neutral disk and canonical vacuum frame, constant near each join. By [F9], the full energy is the slice energy plus nonnegative longitudinal terms, so step 2.1 bounds every competitor below by $T_nL$. Concatenating the two actual collars and the constant middle segment of length $L-2\ell$ gives energy $C_0+T_n(L-2\ell)+C_1$. The collars are constant near their inner faces, so the join is smooth also when the middle length is zero. Taking the infimum gives the claimed uniform $O(1)$ bound. proof_steps.claim: The three-dimensional energy is the transverse planar energy on each slice plus nonnegative longitudinal Maxwell and scalar terms. By [F4] and the definition of $\tau_n$, every competitor has $E_{b,3}\ge\tau_nL$. For each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the definition of the finite infimum provides one planar profile with energy below $\tau_n+\varepsilon$; gauge-clean it by step 5.1. Step 7.1 constructs collars from each fixed end trace to this profile, with one chosen width ell and finite total energy $C_\varepsilon$, independent of L. Concatenate the collars with its translation-invariant extension over length L-2ell. This is a smooth admissible competitor because each collar is constant near the inner face, and it has energy at most $(\tau_n+\varepsilon)(L-2\ell)+C_\varepsilon$. Taking the infimum proves the two-sided bounds. Dividing by L, taking limsup as L tends to infinity and then allowing each $\varepsilon>0$ to tend to zero gives limsup<=tau_n, while the lower bound gives liminf>=tau_n. Hence the limit is tau_n>0. No minimizer or uniform bound on $C_\varepsilon$ as epsilon tends to zero is used, so no generic $O(1)$ remainder follows.

proof_steps.claim: Decompose the integrand into the transverse density $e_\perp(x,z)$, containing $F_{12}$, $D_1q,D_2q$ and the potential, and the nonnegative longitudinal density $e_\parallel(x,z)$, containing $F_{31},F_{32},D_3q$. Since the total density is nonnegative and integrable, [F4] gives $\mathcal E_L=\int_0^L E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)\,dz+\int_{\Omega_L}e_\parallel\,dx\,dz$, where $\mathbf A_\perp=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ and $E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e_\perp(x,z)dx$ for almost every $z$. The slice hypotheses and [F3] give $E(\mathbf A_\perp(\cdot,z),q_z)\ge T_n$ for each slice, while the longitudinal integral is nonnegative; hence $\mathcal E_L\ge T_nL$.

direct_use_reviews.text: [F4] [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: integrable nonnegative energy densities on the polar-coordinate product can be integrated by radial slices; the section integrals are measurable and their total integral equals the plane integral.

proof_steps.claim:
For almost every $r$ larger than the nonzero-field radius, let $Q(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}(|q|^2-\xi)^2ds$ and $K(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}|D_{A,\tau}q|^2ds$, where $D_{A,\tau}$ is the covariant derivative in the unit tangent direction. The potential and kinetic terms of the finite energy, with polar coordinates and [F4], imply $Q,K\in L^1([R_0,\infty))$. For each integer $m\ge1$, the set $S_m=\{r\ge R_0:Q(r)>1/m\}$ has finite measure. Its complement has divergent $\int dr/r$, since removing a finite-measure set from a half-line cannot make the logarithmic integral finite. If $rK(r)\ge1/m$ for every sufficiently large $r\notin S_m$, then $\int K(r)dr\ge m^{-1}\int_{[R,\infty)\setminus S_m}dr/r=\infty$, contradiction. Thus there is an unbounded set of radii with $Q(r)\le1/m$ and $rK(r)<1/m$. By [A1] select an increasing sequence $r_m\to\infty$ from these sets. Along it, [F6] gives $\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\le2\pi\xi r_m+\sqrt{2\pi r_mQ(r_m)}=O(r_m)$, and
$$\left|\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}j\right|\le\left(\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\right)^{1/2}K(r_m)^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$
